skill.name: writing-fragments
skill.description: Interviews writers to discover promising ideas and capture them as unstructured Markdown fragments.
skill.summary: Explore a topic through questions and save useful writing fragments without creating an outline.
skill.author: mattpocock

security_audit.summary: All three static findings are false positives. The apparent command execution is Markdown fencing, and the path question does not perform system reconnaissance.

static_findings.snippet: If the user did not pass a path, ask once where to save the document, then remember it for the rest

finding_verdicts.reason: The backticks at line 44 open a fenced Markdown example that ends at line 67. The block contains document formatting, not Ruby or shell commands.
The backticks at line 67 close the Markdown fence opened at line 44. They are documentation delimiters and do not execute an external command.
Line 13 asks the user where to save output when no path was provided. It does not inspect files, devices, accounts, or host information.

content.value_statement: Early writing ideas often disappear before they become useful material. This skill interviews you, captures promising fragments, and appends them to one Markdown file.
actual_capabilities: Captures the initial prompt and later discussion as reusable writing fragments.
Asks focused questions that expand claims, examples, observations, and possible language.
Appends new fragments to a user-selected Markdown file.
Separates fragments with horizontal rules while avoiding body headings and metadata.
Re-reads the file before writing to preserve changes made outside the conversation.
limitations: Does not create outlines, article structures, or polished final drafts.
Requires the user to choose a destination when no file path is provided.
Does not verify facts, sources, quotations, or technical claims.
Edits existing fragments only when the user gives a specific instruction.

use_cases.title: Explore an essay idea
use_cases.description: Develop an early topic through questions while preserving strong sentences, claims, and examples for later drafting.

use_cases.title: Mine interview insights
use_cases.description: Turn a subject expert conversation into readable fragments without forcing the material into a premature structure.

use_cases.title: Capture technical observations
use_cases.description: Collect explanations, scenarios, code-related insights, and memorable terms before planning a technical article.

prompt_templates.title: Start a fragment session
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me explore an article about [topic]. Save fragments to [path]. Ask questions and capture strong sentences, claims, and examples.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this when you have a topic but little developed material.

prompt_templates.title: Interview an experience
prompt_templates.prompt: Interview me about [experience]. Probe for specific moments, tensions, and lessons. Append each useful fragment to [path] without creating an outline.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this to mine personal or professional experience for an article.

prompt_templates.title: Challenge an argument
prompt_templates.prompt: Explore my claim that [claim]. Question assumptions, request evidence, and test counterexamples. Preserve my strongest language and unresolved thoughts in [path].
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this when an argument needs depth before it receives structure.

prompt_templates.title: Find a leading term
prompt_templates.prompt: Continue exploring [topic] from [path]. Identify recurring ideas and help me name one compact leading term. Keep every result as an independent fragment.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use this advanced prompt to find language that could guide a later draft.

output_examples.input: I want to write about why small software teams often communicate better.
output: Fragment: Every added teammate creates more possible conversations, but not every conversation creates shared understanding.
Fragment: Small teams often move faster because decisions remain visible to everyone who must act on them.

output_examples.input: Explore my experience of replacing weekly status meetings with written updates.
output: Working title: Work That Leaves a Trace
Fragment: The meeting vanished, but its best function remained: everyone could see what had changed.
Fragment: Written updates turned status from a scheduled performance into a durable record.

output_examples.input: Help me find a term for tools that make hidden progress visible.
output: Fragment: A progress signal is any artifact that shows movement before the final result exists.
Fragment: The best progress signals reduce uncertainty without demanding another meeting.

best_practices: Choose a dedicated Markdown file and keep its path stable during the session.
Answer questions with concrete events, exact language, and unresolved tensions.
Review fragments between turns and request precise cuts, merges, or rewrites.
anti_patterns: Do not ask for an outline or final draft during fragment exploration.
Do not place unrelated projects in the same fragment file.
Do not treat generated claims or quotations as verified facts.

faq.question: What is a writing fragment?
faq.answer: A fragment is a readable piece of potential draft material, such as a claim, example, quotation, scene, or unfinished thought.

faq.question: Does this skill create an outline?
faq.answer: No. It explores possible material without choosing sections, order, or a final argument.

faq.question: Where does the skill save fragments?
faq.answer: It appends fragments to the Markdown path you provide. It asks for a path once when none is supplied.

faq.question: Will it preserve my file edits?
faq.answer: Yes. It re-reads the file before each write and preserves changes you made between turns.

faq.question: Can I revise an existing fragment?
faq.answer: Yes. Request a specific cut, rewrite, or merge, and identify the fragment clearly.

faq.question: Does it verify facts and sources?
faq.answer: No. Review all factual claims, quotations, and sources before using fragments in published work.
